outline.title: Abstract
outline.description: This section will provide a concise summary of the entire survey, highlighting the rapid evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) security from 2023 to 2026. It will synthesize the shift from static, unimodal vulnerabilities to dynamic, multimodal, and agentic adversarial arms races. The abstract will briefly touch upon the four core categories analyzed: Data and Model Poisoning, Adversarial Attacks, Prompt Injection, and LLM Hallucinations, outlining the survey's contribution in systematizing threat models, testing methodologies, and cross-cutting defenses.

outline.title: Introduction
outline.description: The introduction will establish the motivation for the survey, detailing the critical need for robust LLM security as models are deployed in high-stakes domains. It will outline the scope of the paper, synthesizing insights from over 80 recent studies (2023-2026). The narrative must emphasize the chronological transition from early baseline vulnerability identification (e.g., simple text-based jailbreaks) to the current state of highly sophisticated, automated, and co-evolutionary adversarial attacks. Finally, it will summarize the paper's core contributions, including a unified taxonomy of threats, a comprehensive review of testing methodologies, and an analysis of emerging defense paradigms.

outline.title: Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: This section will establish the foundational concepts and terminology used throughout the survey. It must define key terms such as Jailbreak, Prompt Injection (Direct vs. Indirect), Attack Success Rate (ASR), Safety Alignment (RLHF, DPO), and Guardrails. Furthermore, it will provide a brief overview of standard LLM and MLLM architectures to contextualize where vulnerabilities arise. Crucially, it will introduce a unified threat model that categorizes vulnerabilities into training-time threats (e.g., data poisoning, backdoors) and inference-time threats (e.g., adversarial attacks, prompt injection, hallucinations), setting the structural stage for the subsequent core sections.

outline.title: Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
outline.description: This section will explore the evolution of data and model poisoning attacks from 2024 to 2025. It must detail the initial 2024 focus on systematizing and benchmarking generative backdoors in open-source models like LLaMA-2, Mistral, and GPT-J, specifically citing the foundational frameworks established by [Chowdhury_2024_Breaking] and [Li_2024_Backdoorllm]. The narrative should then transition to the late 2024/2025 turning point, where attacks expanded beyond unimodal text into complex multimodal and embodied AI vectors. A critical focus must be placed on the exploitation of alignment and retrieval mechanisms, particularly highlighting vulnerabilities within the Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) pipeline.

outline.title: Inference-Time Threats I: Adversarial Attacks
outline.description: This section will cover the landscape of adversarial attacks on LLMs and MLLMs, tracing its rapid evolution between 2024 and 2026. It must begin by discussing the 2024 baseline vulnerabilities in high-stakes, specialized domains, explicitly referencing [Yang_2024_Adversarial] to illustrate the susceptibility of models processing sensitive healthcare datasets like MIMIC-III. The discussion should then map the transition from these domain-specific exploits to a sophisticated, multi-faceted arms race involving advanced offensive weaponization. The section will also introduce early defensive wrappers, such as the contrastive prompt tuning mechanism for detecting black-box attacks proposed by [Wang_2024_Advqdet].

outline.title: Inference-Time Threats II: Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: Given the massive volume of research (54 papers), this section will provide an in-depth analysis of prompt injection and jailbreak attacks, focusing on the transformative 2025-2026 period. It must document the definitive shift from static, rule-based defenses to a highly dynamic, automated adversarial arms race. The text must explicitly detail how attackers utilize adaptive optimization techniques, including modified Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) fuzzing, and genetic algorithms, to achieve 50% to 71% ASR against state-of-the-art agents, citing [Zhan_2025_LLM], [Wang_2025_LLM], and [Maloyan_2025_LLM]. The section should conclude by discussing the bifurcation of recent research into extreme computational efficiency and dynamic, ensemble-based attack systems.

outline.title: Intrinsic Vulnerabilities: LLM Hallucinations
outline.description: This section will analyze the evolution of LLM hallucinations and factual consistency research from 2023 to 2026. It must describe the 2023 paradigm of using LLMs as evaluators to police themselves, highlighting the introduction of zero-shot inference-time methods. The narrative must explicitly cite the development of ChainPoll by [Friel_2023_LLM], detailing how polling and Chain-of-Thought prompting optimized inference costs while outperforming competitors. The section should then trace the conceptual maturation in 2024, where the field moved away from treating non-factual generations as simple binary errors toward more mechanistically informed and conceptually nuanced frameworks.

outline.title: Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: This section will synthesize defensive strategies across the entire threat spectrum, highlighting the transition from early 'patchwork' solutions to integrated security architectures. It will discuss the 2024 reliance on external stateful detection and prompt-level manipulations, referencing the contrastive prompt tuning by [Wang_2024_Advqdet]. It will then cover the evolution of guardrails, perplexity filters, and robust alignment techniques (like DPO). The narrative must emphasize the growing consensus in 2025-2026 that static defenses are inadequate, driving the development of dynamic, ensemble-based defensive systems capable of countering automated optimization attacks like GCG and MCTS.

outline.title: Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
outline.description: This MANDATORY section will provide a comprehensive, cross-category overview of how LLM security is evaluated. It must detail the specific benchmarks, datasets, metrics, and tools used across all threat vectors. For Prompt Injection and Adversarial Attacks, it will discuss Attack Success Rate (ASR) and standard red-teaming benchmarks (e.g., AdvBench). For Data Poisoning, it will cover backdoor trigger evaluation frameworks and metrics for measuring alignment degradation. For Hallucinations, it will detail factual consistency metrics and LLM-as-a-judge polling methodologies. The section must critically assess the limitations of current static benchmarks in the face of dynamic, automated attacks.

outline.title: Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: This section will critically analyze the gaps and limitations in the current LLM security landscape. It will discuss the fundamental inadequacy of static guardrails against co-evolutionary adversarial algorithms and the theoretical limits of safety alignment (RLHF). Open challenges to be highlighted include securing multimodal and embodied AI systems against complex poisoning attacks, the computational overhead of dynamic ensemble defenses, and the lack of standardized, dynamic benchmarks that can keep pace with automated red-teaming tools. It will propose future research directions to address these critical vulnerabilities.

outline.title: Conclusion
outline.description: The conclusion will synthesize the primary findings of the survey, reiterating the paradigm shift from isolated, unimodal vulnerabilities to a complex, automated adversarial arms race in LLM security. It will provide actionable, practical recommendations for researchers and practitioners deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments, emphasizing the necessity of adopting dynamic, multi-layered, and mechanistically informed security frameworks rather than relying on static, bolt-on defenses.
